lesson.title: Python Overview and the Execution Model
objectives: Describe what Python is and why it is popular for back-end, automation and data work.
Explain how CPython compiles source code to bytecode and runs it on a virtual machine.
Distinguish compile-time errors (SyntaxError) from run-time errors (NameError, TypeError).
Explain the role of __name__ == '__main__' and .pyc caching.
Answer the classic 'Is Python compiled or interpreted?' interview question precisely.
lesson.definition: Python is a high-level, general-purpose, dynamically typed programming language that emphasises readability. The standard implementation, CPython, first compiles a source file into bytecode (a low-level, platform-independent instruction set) and then executes that bytecode on the Python Virtual Machine, an interpreter loop written in C.

theory.heading: What Python is and why companies use it
theory.body: Python was created by Guido van Rossum and first released in 1991. Its design favours readable code, a large standard library ('batteries included') and fast development over raw execution speed. That trade-off is why it dominates scripting, web back ends (Django, Flask, FastAPI), data engineering, machine learning and test automation: developer time is usually more expensive than CPU time, and performance-critical parts can be delegated to C extensions such as NumPy.
points: High-level: memory management, garbage collection and data structures are built in.
Dynamically typed: types belong to objects, not variables, and are checked at run time.
Multi-paradigm: procedural, object-oriented and functional styles are all supported.
Python 2 reached end of life in 2020; interviews assume Python 3.

theory.heading: Compiled or interpreted? Both
theory.body: When you run python app.py, CPython reads the whole file, tokenises and parses it into an abstract syntax tree, and compiles that tree into bytecode. Only then does the Python Virtual Machine (PVM) start executing the bytecode instruction by instruction. So Python is compiled to bytecode and the bytecode is interpreted. It is not compiled to native machine code ahead of time the way C is.
points: Source (.py) -> tokens -> AST -> bytecode (code objects) -> executed by the PVM.
Because the whole file is compiled first, a SyntaxError anywhere stops the program before line 1 runs.
Name lookups, attribute access and type checks happen at run time, so a NameError only appears when that line executes.
The dis module shows the bytecode: import dis; dis.dis(func).

theory.heading: Bytecode caching and .pyc files
theory.body: When a module is imported, CPython saves its compiled bytecode in a __pycache__ folder as a .pyc file named for the interpreter version, for example utils.cpython-311.pyc. On the next import, if the source has not changed, Python skips compilation and loads the cached bytecode. This speeds up start-up, not execution. The main script you run directly is compiled every time and is not cached.
points: .pyc files are a start-up optimisation, not a way to hide or speed up code.
They are version-specific, which is why the interpreter tag is in the file name.
Deleting __pycache__ is always safe; Python regenerates it.

theory.heading: Implementations and the __main__ module
theory.body: Python is a language specification with several implementations: CPython (the reference, written in C), PyPy (a JIT compiler that can make long-running pure-Python code much faster), Jython (JVM) and MicroPython (microcontrollers). Whichever implementation runs it, the file you execute directly becomes the module named __main__. The idiom if __name__ == '__main__': lets a file act both as an importable module and as a script: the guarded code runs only when the file is executed directly.
points: Imported module: __name__ is the module's name, e.g. 'utils'.
Executed script: __name__ is '__main__'.
Put test calls and CLI entry points under the guard so imports have no side effects.

theory.heading: Strengths and limitations to state in interviews
theory.body: Python's strengths are readability, a huge ecosystem, rapid prototyping and portability. Its limitations are slower CPU-bound execution than compiled languages, the Global Interpreter Lock that prevents CPython threads from running Python bytecode in parallel, higher memory use per object and run-time rather than compile-time type errors. Good engineers mitigate these with profiling, C-backed libraries, multiprocessing, and type hints checked by tools such as mypy.
points: Everything is an object, including functions, classes and modules.
Indentation is syntax: blocks are defined by consistent indentation, not braces.
Type hints are optional annotations; the interpreter does not enforce them.

example.title: A module that is also a script
example.body: This file defines a reusable function and runs a quick demo only when executed directly. Another file can import greet without printing anything, because in that case __name__ is 'greetings', not '__main__'.

code.source:
# greetings.py
def greet(name):
    return f'Hello, {name}!'

print('module name:', __name__)

if __name__ == '__main__':
    print(greet('Asha'))

# python greetings.py      -> module name: __main__ / Hello, Asha!
# >>> import greetings      -> module name: greetings

demonstration.description: Use the dis module to see the bytecode CPython generates for a tiny function. Exact opcode names differ between Python versions (for example BINARY_ADD in 3.8 became BINARY_OP in 3.11), which is exactly why bytecode is an implementation detail rather than part of the language.

code.source:

def add(a, b):

takeaways: CPython compiles source to bytecode, then the Python Virtual Machine interprets the bytecode.
A SyntaxError anywhere in a file prevents any of it from running; NameError and TypeError appear only when the line executes.
.pyc files in __pycache__ cache bytecode of imported modules to speed up start-up.
if __name__ == '__main__': separates script behaviour from importable code.
Python trades raw CPU speed for readability and productivity; heavy lifting is delegated to C extensions.
CPython, PyPy, Jython and MicroPython are different implementations of the same language.

interview.question: Is Python a compiled or an interpreted language?
interview.answer: Both, in the CPython implementation. Source code is compiled to bytecode, and the bytecode is executed by the Python Virtual Machine, an interpreter. It is not compiled ahead of time to native machine code.
interview.explanation: Saying only 'interpreted' is the common weak answer. A strong answer names the pipeline (source -> AST -> bytecode -> PVM) and mentions that PyPy adds JIT compilation.

interview.question: What is the purpose of if __name__ == '__main__':?
interview.answer: It runs the guarded block only when the file is executed directly. When the file is imported, __name__ is the module name, so the block is skipped and importing has no side effects.
interview.explanation: Mention practical uses: CLI entry points, quick demos and avoiding duplicate work when multiprocessing re-imports the main module on Windows.

interview.question: What are .pyc files and __pycache__?
interview.answer: .pyc files hold the compiled bytecode of imported modules, stored in __pycache__ with a version tag. Python reuses them when the source is unchanged, which speeds up imports. They do not make code run faster once loaded.
interview.explanation: Interviewers check that you know caching affects start-up time only, and that the main script is not cached.

interview.question: A file has a syntax error on its last line. Does the first print statement run?
interview.answer: No. The whole file is parsed and compiled before execution starts, so the SyntaxError is raised before any statement runs. A NameError on the last line, by contrast, would only occur after the earlier lines had executed.
interview.explanation: This tests real understanding of the execution model: compile-time versus run-time errors.

interview.question: What are the main limitations of Python, and how do teams work around them?
interview.answer: CPU-bound code is slower than in compiled languages, the GIL stops threads running Python bytecode in parallel, objects use more memory and type errors surface at run time. Teams use C-backed libraries (NumPy), multiprocessing or native extensions for speed, PyPy for some workloads, and type hints with mypy plus tests for correctness.
interview.explanation: Balanced answers that pair each limitation with a mitigation sound like real engineering experience.

practice.title: Syntax checker without running the code
practice.objective: Use Python's compile step to detect syntax errors before execution, mirroring how CPython compiles a whole file before running it.
practice.statement: Read a small Python program and report whether it compiles. Do not execute it. If it compiles, print OK followed by the number of non-blank lines. If it does not, print the line number of the syntax error reported by the compiler. IndentationError is a kind of SyntaxError and must be reported the same way.
practice.input_format: The first line is an integer N. The next N lines are the program's source code (indentation preserved).
practice.output_format: Either 'OK <k>' where k is the number of non-blank source lines, or 'SyntaxError on line <L>'.
constraints: Use compile(source, '<input>', 'exec'); never call exec or eval on the input.
A line containing only spaces counts as blank.
practice.starter:
import sys

lines = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
n = int(lines[0])
code_lines = lines[1:n + 1]
source = '\n'.join(code_lines) + '\n'

# TODO: compile the source and print the result
practice.solution:
import sys

lines = sys.stdin.read().split('\n')
n = int(lines[0])
code_lines = lines[1:n + 1]
source = '\n'.join(code_lines) + '\n'

try:
    compile(source, '<input>', 'exec')
except SyntaxError as err:
    print(f'SyntaxError on line {err.lineno}')
else:
    non_blank = sum(1 for line in code_lines if line.strip())
    print(f'OK {non_blank}')
explanation: Read all input and keep exactly N source lines, preserving their indentation.
compile() runs the tokenizer, parser and bytecode compiler but executes nothing, just like the first phase of python file.py.
Catch SyntaxError; IndentationError and TabError are subclasses, so one except clause handles all of them. err.lineno holds the line number.
In the else block (no exception), count lines whose strip() is non-empty and print OK with the count.

print(add(2, 3))

quiz.question: What does CPython produce from a .py source file before executing it?
options: Bytecode that runs on the Python Virtual Machine
Native machine code for the current CPU
quiz.explanation: CPython compiles source to bytecode, which its virtual machine then interprets. PyPy can JIT-compile further, but CPython does not produce native code.

quiz.question: What does this program print when run as a script?
quiz.code:
print('start')

def report():
    return missing_variable

print('end')
options: start and end on two lines
quiz.explanation: Names inside a function body are looked up only when the function runs. report() is never called, so no NameError occurs and both lines print.

quiz.question: utils.py ends with print('loaded'). You want the message only when running python utils.py, not when another file imports utils. What should you do?
options: Wrap the print in a try/except block
quiz.explanation: When imported, __name__ is 'utils'; when run directly, it is '__main__'. The guard runs the code only in the second case.

quiz.question: What is the main benefit of the .pyc files stored in __pycache__?
options: They hide source code from other developers
They allow Python 3.8 bytecode to run on Python 3.12
They skip recompilation on import, so start-up is faster
quiz.explanation: Cached bytecode avoids reparsing unchanged modules. Execution speed is the same, and .pyc files are version-specific.

quiz.question: A 200-line script has a missing colon on line 200. What happens when you run it?
options: A SyntaxError is raised and no line runs
Python skips line 200 and finishes normally
Lines 1 to 199 run, then a SyntaxError is raised
quiz.explanation: The whole file is compiled before execution starts, so a syntax error anywhere prevents every line from running.

lesson.title: Variables, Dynamic Typing and Object References
objectives: Explain that Python variables are names bound to objects, not boxes holding values.
Contrast dynamic typing with static typing and strong typing with weak typing.
Use id(), type(), isinstance(), == and is correctly.
Predict the effect of assignment, rebinding and in-place mutation on shared objects.
Recognise interning and small-integer caching as implementation details.
lesson.definition: In Python a variable is a name that refers to an object stored in memory. Assignment binds a name to an object; it never copies the object. Python is dynamically typed, meaning the type belongs to the object and is checked at run time, so the same name can refer to an int now and a string later.

theory.heading: Names, objects and binding
theory.body: Every value in Python is an object with three properties: an identity (where it lives, shown by id()), a type (shown by type()) and a value. A statement such as x = 42 creates or finds the int object 42 and binds the name x to it. Writing y = x does not copy 42; it binds a second name to the same object. Thinking of variables as labels or sticky notes, rather than boxes, explains most surprising behaviour beginners meet with lists and dictionaries.
points: Assignment binds a name; it never copies data.
id(obj) returns an integer unique among objects alive at the same time (the memory address in CPython).
A name can be rebound to a different object at any time with another assignment.
del x removes the name, not necessarily the object; the object is freed when nothing refers to it.

theory.heading: Dynamic and strong typing
theory.body: Python is dynamically typed: you never declare a type, and type checks happen when operations run. It is also strongly typed: Python does not silently convert unrelated types, so '3' + 4 raises TypeError instead of producing '34' or 7. Interviewers like this distinction because many candidates wrongly call Python 'weakly typed'. Optional type hints such as def area(r: float) -> float document intent and are checked by external tools like mypy, but the interpreter ignores them at run time.
points: Dynamic: types are attached to objects and checked at run time.
Strong: no implicit conversion between unrelated types such as str and int.
Numeric types do widen automatically: 1 + 2.5 gives 3.5.
Type hints improve tooling and readability but do not enforce anything.

theory.heading: == versus is
theory.body: == compares values by calling the __eq__ method, while is compares identity, that is, whether two names refer to the very same object. Two separate lists [1, 2] are equal but not identical. Use is only for singletons such as None, True and False (x is None is the idiomatic check) and use == for comparing data. Relying on is for numbers or strings is a bug that may appear to work because of caching.
points: a == b: do the objects have equal values?
a is b: are a and b the same object (same id)?
Always write x is None, never x == None.
isinstance(x, (int, float)) is preferred over type(x) == int because it respects inheritance.

theory.heading: Caching and interning are implementation details
theory.body: CPython pre-creates the integers from -5 to 256 and reuses them, and it interns some strings that look like identifiers. As a result, a = 100; b = 100; a is b is usually True, while the same test with 1000 can be True or False depending on how the code was compiled. These are optimisations, not language guarantees, so correct code never depends on them.
points: Small int cache: -5 to 256 in CPython.
String interning: compile-time identifier-like strings, or explicit sys.intern().
Never use is to compare numbers or strings.

theory.heading: Multiple assignment, unpacking and swapping
theory.body: Python evaluates the whole right-hand side before binding names, which makes tuple unpacking safe for swaps: a, b = b, a needs no temporary variable. Starred unpacking collects the rest: first, *rest = [1, 2, 3]. Chained assignment a = b = [] binds both names to one list, a common source of shared-state bugs.
points: a, b = b, a swaps by building a tuple first.
x = y = [] makes x and y refer to the same list.
Names are case-sensitive and must not start with a digit; follow snake_case per PEP 8.

example.title: Rebinding versus mutating
example.body: Both names start out pointing to the same list. Mutating through one name is visible through the other, but rebinding one name to a new object breaks the link without affecting the other name.

code.source:
scores = [70, 85]
backup = scores            # same list, two names
backup.append(90)          # mutate the shared object
print(scores)              # [70, 85, 90]

backup = [0]               # rebind backup to a new list
print(scores, backup)      # [70, 85, 90] [0]
print(scores is backup)    # False

print(type(x).__name__)     # int
x = 'ten'
print(type(x).__name__)     # str  (same name, new object)

b = [1, 2]
c = a

str
True False

takeaways: Variables are names bound to objects; assignment never copies.
Python is dynamically and strongly typed.
== compares values; is compares identity. Use is only with None, True and False.
Mutating a shared object is visible through every name that refers to it; rebinding is not.
Small-integer caching and string interning are CPython optimisations, not guarantees.
Type hints are documentation for tools; the interpreter does not enforce them.

interview.question: What does it mean that Python is dynamically typed?
interview.answer: Types are attached to objects rather than variables and are checked at run time. A name can refer to an int and later to a str, and you never declare types.
interview.explanation: Add that Python is still strongly typed ('3' + 4 raises TypeError) to stand out.

interview.question: What is the difference between == and is?
interview.answer: == checks whether two objects have equal values (via __eq__). is checks whether two names refer to the same object in memory. Use is for None and other singletons.
interview.explanation: Give the list example: [1] == [1] is True, [1] is [1] is False.

interview.question: Why might a = 256; b = 256; a is b be True but the same test with 257 be False?
interview.answer: CPython caches small integers from -5 to 256, so both names get the same cached object. Larger integers may be created separately, so identity is not guaranteed. This is an implementation detail, and numbers should always be compared with ==.
interview.explanation: Interviewers want you to know the reason and the lesson: never rely on is for value comparison.

interview.question: After a = [1, 2]; b = a; b += [3], what is a? What if the lists were tuples?
interview.answer: a is [1, 2, 3] because += on a list mutates it in place and both names share it. With tuples, b += (3,) creates a new tuple and rebinds b, so a stays (1, 2).
interview.explanation: This shows you understand that += calls __iadd__ when available (mutable types) and falls back to creating a new object for immutable types.

interview.question: Are type hints enforced at run time? Why use them?
interview.answer: No. The interpreter stores them in __annotations__ but does not check them. They are used by static checkers (mypy, pyright), IDEs and frameworks such as FastAPI and pydantic, which read them deliberately to validate data.
interview.explanation: Mentioning that some libraries opt in to run-time validation shows current, practical knowledge.

practice.title: Literal type inspector
practice.objective: Practise reasoning about the run-time type of values and whether each type is mutable.
practice.statement: Each input line contains one Python literal. For each line print the name of its type and whether that type is mutable or immutable. Parse literals safely with ast.literal_eval instead of eval. Treat list, dict and set as mutable; every other type produced by a literal is immutable.
practice.input_format: The first line is N. Each of the next N lines holds one valid Python literal.

example.output:
int immutable
str immutable
list mutable
NoneType immutable

constraints: Literals may be int, float, complex, str, bytes, bool, None, list, tuple, dict or set.
Use type(value).__name__ for the type name.
practice.starter:
import ast

n = int(input())
for _ in range(n):
    value = ast.literal_eval(input().strip())
    # TODO: print the type name and mutability
practice.solution:
import ast

MUTABLE = (list, dict, set)

n = int(input())
for _ in range(n):
    value = ast.literal_eval(input().strip())
    kind = 'mutable' if isinstance(value, MUTABLE) else 'immutable'
    print(type(value).__name__, kind)
explanation: ast.literal_eval turns text such as "[1, 2]" into the real object without executing arbitrary code, which makes it safe for untrusted input.
type(value).__name__ gives the class name, for example 'int' or 'NoneType'.
isinstance with a tuple of the mutable built-in types decides the label.
True and False print as bool because type() reports the exact class, even though bool is a subclass of int.

quiz.question: A function returns None when a record is missing. Which check is the idiomatic way to test the result?
quiz.explanation: None is a singleton, so identity comparison with is is correct, fast and cannot be fooled by a custom __eq__.

lesson.title: Numbers and Strings: Slicing, Formatting and Methods
objectives: Use int, float, complex and Decimal appropriately and explain floating-point error.
Slice strings with start, stop and step, including negative indices.
Format output with f-strings and format specifiers.
Apply common string methods: split, join, strip, replace, find, startswith, upper and title.
Explain why strings are immutable and why ''.join is preferred over += in loops.
lesson.definition: Python's numeric types are int (arbitrary precision integers), float (64-bit IEEE 754 binary floating point) and complex, with Decimal and Fraction available in the standard library for exact arithmetic. A str is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters that supports indexing, slicing, a rich set of methods and formatted string literals (f-strings).

theory.heading: Numbers: int, float, Decimal
theory.body: Python ints never overflow: 2 ** 100 is computed exactly because ints grow as needed. Floats are binary approximations, so 0.1 + 0.2 is 0.30000000000000004 and equality tests on floats are unreliable. For money, store whole paise or cents as ints, or use decimal.Decimal built from strings. Compare floats with math.isclose. Division / always returns a float, // performs floor division and round() uses banker's rounding (round half to even), so round(2.5) is 2.
points: int: unlimited size; float: about 15-17 significant digits.
math.isclose(a, b) for float comparison.
Decimal('0.1') is exact; Decimal(0.1) inherits the float's error.
int('42'), float('3.5') and str(7) convert explicitly; int('3.5') raises ValueError.

theory.heading: Indexing and slicing
theory.body: Strings are sequences, so s[i] returns one character and negative indices count from the end (s[-1] is the last character). A slice s[start:stop:step] returns a new string from start up to but not including stop. Missing values default to the beginning, end and step 1, and out-of-range slice bounds are clipped instead of raising errors. s[::-1] reverses a string, a common interview one-liner for palindrome checks.
points: s[0:3] or s[:3]: first three characters.
s[-3:]: last three characters.
s[::2]: every second character.
s[10] on a short string raises IndexError, but s[10:20] returns ''.

theory.heading: Immutability and efficient building
theory.body: Strings cannot be changed in place: s[0] = 'J' raises TypeError, and every method such as upper() or replace() returns a new string. Building a large string with += in a loop can create many intermediate strings, which is quadratic in the worst case. Collect pieces in a list and call ''.join(pieces) once; it computes the total length and copies each piece only once.
points: Methods return new strings; assign the result: s = s.strip().
Use sep.join(iterable_of_strings) to concatenate many parts.
Immutability makes strings hashable, so they can be dictionary keys.

theory.heading: Essential string methods
theory.body: Most text processing in interviews uses a small set of methods. split() without arguments splits on any run of whitespace and drops empty strings, while split(',') splits on every comma exactly. strip() removes surrounding whitespace, find() returns -1 when not found whereas index() raises ValueError, and in tests substring membership.
points: Cleaning: strip, lstrip, rstrip, lower, upper, title, casefold.
Searching: in, find, index, count, startswith, endswith.
Transforming: replace, split, join, zfill, center.
Checking: isdigit, isalpha, isalnum, isspace.

theory.heading: Formatting output with f-strings
theory.body: f-strings (Python 3.6+) evaluate expressions inside braces at run time and accept a format specifier after a colon: {value:<width}, {value:>width}, {value:^width} for alignment, {value:.2f} for fixed decimals, {value:,} for thousands separators, {value:05d} for zero padding and {value:%} for percentages. Python 3.8 added the debugging form {x=}, which prints both the expression and its value.
points: f'{price:.2f}' -> two decimal places.
f'{name:<10}|' -> left-align in 10 characters.
Older styles: '%s' % x and '{}'.format(x) still appear in legacy code.

lesson.title: Operators, Expressions and Precedence
objectives: Use arithmetic operators correctly, including floor division and modulo with negative numbers.
Explain short-circuit evaluation and why and/or return operands rather than booleans.
Read chained comparisons and operator precedence without guessing.
Apply bitwise operators to classic interview tasks.
Use the walrus operator := and augmented assignment appropriately.
lesson.definition: An operator is a symbol or keyword that combines values (operands) into an expression that Python evaluates to a single object. Python groups operators into arithmetic, comparison, logical, bitwise, identity, membership and assignment operators, and evaluates them according to fixed precedence and associativity rules.

theory.heading: Arithmetic: /, //, % and **
theory.body: The / operator always performs true division and returns a float, even for 6 / 3. Floor division // rounds toward negative infinity, not toward zero, so -7 // 2 is -4. The modulo operator % is defined so that (a // b) * b + (a % b) == a, which means the result takes the sign of the divisor: -7 % 2 is 1. This differs from C and Java, and it is why Python's % is convenient for wrapping indices and clock arithmetic. divmod(a, b) returns both results at once.
points: ** is right-associative: 2 ** 3 ** 2 = 2 ** 9 = 512.
Unary minus binds looser than **: -2 ** 2 = -4.

theory.heading: Comparison and chaining
theory.body: Comparisons return True or False and can be chained: a < b < c means a < b and b < c, with b evaluated only once. Chaining works with any comparison operators, so 1 < 3 > 2 is True even though it reads oddly. Comparing incompatible types such as 3 < 'a' raises TypeError in Python 3, unlike Python 2.
points: 0 <= index < len(items) is the idiomatic range check.
== compares values, is compares identity, in tests membership.
Sequences compare lexicographically: [1, 2] < [1, 3] and 'apple' < 'banana'.

theory.heading: Logical operators and short-circuiting
theory.body: and, or and not work on truthiness. and returns the first falsy operand or the last operand; or returns the first truthy operand or the last operand. Evaluation stops as soon as the result is known, which is called short-circuiting. That is why name = user_input or 'Guest' supplies a default, and why items and items[0] is safe for an empty list. not always returns a real bool.
points: Falsy values: None, False, 0, 0.0, '', [], (), {}, set().
Put cheap or guarding conditions first: if user and user.is_admin.

theory.heading: Bitwise operators
theory.body: &, |, ^, ~, << and >> operate on the binary representation of integers. They appear in interview questions about flags, permissions and tricks: n & 1 tests odd or even, n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit (so it is 0 exactly when a positive n is a power of two), x ^ x is 0 (used to find the single non-duplicated number), and n << k multiplies by 2 to the power k. ~n equals -n - 1 because Python ints behave like infinite two's complement.
points: Count set bits: bin(n).count('1') (or n.bit_count() in 3.10+).
a ^ b ^ a == b: XOR cancels pairs.

theory.heading: Precedence, assignment expressions and augmented assignment
theory.body: From highest to lowest the key levels are: ** ; unary - and ~ ; * / // % ; + - ; shifts ; & ; ^ ; | ; comparisons (including in and is) ; not ; and ; or ; the conditional expression ; and finally :=. When in doubt, add parentheses: readable code beats clever code. The walrus operator := (Python 3.8) assigns inside an expression, for example while (line := f.readline()):. Augmented assignment such as x += 1 may mutate in place for mutable types.
points: not a == b means not (a == b).
a if condition else b is Python's ternary expression.
Walrus avoids computing a value twice: if (n := len(data)) > 10: print(n).

hours, minutes = divmod(135, 60)
print(hours, minutes)           # 2 15

interview.question: What is the difference between / and // in Python 3?
interview.answer: / is true division and always returns a float. // is floor division: it rounds the result down toward negative infinity, returning an int for int operands, so -7 // 2 is -4.
interview.explanation: Mentioning the negative-number behaviour separates a strong answer from a memorised one.

interview.question: What does 'a or b' return?
interview.answer: It returns a if a is truthy, otherwise b. It does not convert the result to a bool, and b is not evaluated when a is truthy.
interview.explanation: Link it to idioms such as name = value or 'default', and warn that 0 or '' are also replaced, which may be unintended.

interview.question: What does 1 < 3 > 2 evaluate to, and why?

interview.question: What is the walrus operator and when would you use it?

lesson.title: Control Flow: Conditionals, Loops and Loop Control
objectives: Write if/elif/else chains that choose between mutually exclusive branches.
Iterate over sequences and ranges with for loops and use while for sentinel-driven repetition.
Use break, continue and the loop else clause to control iteration precisely.
Explain when the else attached to a loop runs and why it pairs with break.
Recognise pitfalls such as mutating a list while iterating over it.
lesson.definition: Control flow is the order in which a program's statements run. Python selects a branch with the conditional statement if/elif/else, which tests truthiness, and repeats work with two loops: for, which visits each item of an iterable in turn, and while, which repeats as long as a condition stays true. break, continue and the optional else clause attached to a loop give fine-grained control over how iteration ends.

theory.heading: Conditionals and truthiness
theory.body: An if statement runs its block only when the condition is truthy. Because every object has a truth value, you rarely need to compare against True or False: empty collections, 0, 0.0, None and the empty string are falsy and most other objects are truthy. Use elif for additional mutually exclusive tests and a final else for the fallback. Python has no switch statement, so a chain of elif or a dictionary that maps keys to functions is the usual replacement. The conditional expression value_if_true if condition else value_if_false is a compact single-expression form.
points: Falsy values: None, False, 0, 0.0, '', [], (), {}, set().
Order matters: test the most specific condition first.
Guard clauses (early return) keep deep nesting out of functions.
a if cond else b selects a value, not a block of statements.

theory.heading: for loops and range
theory.body: A for loop iterates directly over any iterable, asking it for the next item until it is exhausted, so for item in items is clearer and safer than indexing. range(stop), range(start, stop) and range(start, stop, step) produce a lazy sequence of integers and never include stop. When you need both the index and the value, use enumerate(iterable, start=0); when you need to walk two sequences together, use zip. The loop target can unpack tuples, for example for key, value in pairs:. Iterating directly also works on strings, dictionaries, sets, files and generators.
points: range(3) yields 0, 1, 2.
enumerate gives (index, value) pairs without a manual counter.
zip stops at the shortest of its inputs.
Unpacking in the loop target mirrors tuple assignment.

theory.heading: while loops and sentinels
theory.body: A while loop re-tests its condition before every pass, so it fits situations where the number of iterations is unknown: reading until end of input, retrying until success, or advancing a value until it reaches a target. Always make sure something inside the body moves the loop toward termination, otherwise it runs forever. A common pattern is while True: with an explicit break, and while (line := reader.readline()): to stop at an empty string. Remember that the condition is re-evaluated each time, unlike a one-off if test.
points: Update the loop variable inside the body so the loop can end.
while True plus break is a readable loop-until-done idiom.
continue skips the rest of a pass and re-tests the condition.
Avoid busy loops that spin without doing useful work.

theory.heading: break, continue and the loop else clause
theory.body: break exits the innermost loop immediately, continue skips the remaining statements of the current pass but keeps looping, and both affect only the nearest enclosing loop. Python's unusual loop else clause runs only if the loop finished normally, that is without hitting a break. It is the idiomatic way to express searched for something and did not find it, because code after the loop cannot tell whether a break occurred. In nested loops break leaves only one level, so a flag variable or a function with return is often cleaner.
points: break ends the loop; continue starts the next iteration.
The else block is skipped whenever break runs.
Use a search loop with else instead of a found flag.
return inside a function exits the whole function, not just the loop.

theory.heading: Common pitfalls
theory.body: Removing items from a list while iterating over it skips elements because the indices shift; iterate over a copy, build a new list, or collect the items to delete first. Off-by-one errors are common when translating between range and inclusive bounds. Changing the size of a dictionary or set during iteration raises RuntimeError. Finally, a for loop over an empty iterable simply does nothing, yet its else clause still runs, which can surprise people who expect the block to be tied to the body executing.
points: Iterate over list(items) when deleting, or build a filtered list.
range(n) covers 0 to n-1, not n.
A for loop over an empty sequence runs zero times but its else still runs.
break in a nested loop exits only the inner loop.

Use for over iterables and while when the number of iterations is unknown.
break stops the innermost loop; continue skips to the next pass.
A loop else runs only when no break occurred, making it ideal for searches.

interview.question: What is the difference between break and continue?
interview.answer: break exits the innermost loop immediately. continue skips the remaining statements of the current iteration and moves straight to the next pass, where the loop condition is tested again.
interview.explanation: Mention that neither statement affects an outer loop, which is a common follow-up question about nested loops.

interview.question: What does the else clause on a for or while loop do?
interview.answer: It runs after the loop finishes normally, meaning only if the loop was not exited with break. It is typically used to handle the not-found case of a search without a flag variable.
interview.explanation: A strong answer contrasts it with the if/else else and gives a search example such as for/else over a list of records.

interview.question: How do you loop with an index in Python, and why avoid range(len(items))?
interview.answer: Use for i, item in enumerate(items). range(len(items)) works but is less readable and error-prone because you index the sequence yourself and lose the direct reference to the item.
interview.explanation: enumerate also accepts a start value, which is handy for numbering lines starting at one.

interview.question: Why does deleting items from a list while looping over it skip elements?
interview.answer: Removing an element shifts every later element one position left, but the iterator's internal index still moves forward, so the element that slid into the current position is never visited. Iterate over a copy, delete in reverse, or build a new list instead.
interview.explanation: The same class of bug affects any sequence whose length changes during iteration.

interview.question: When would you choose while over for?
interview.answer: When the number of iterations is not known in advance, for example reading until a sentinel value, retrying an operation until it succeeds, or advancing a value until some condition holds. for is preferable whenever you are walking over the items of an iterable.
interview.explanation: Interviewers like to hear that for loops are implemented on top of the iterator protocol and handling IndexError manually is not idiomatic.

lesson.title: Functions: Parameters, Arguments and Return Values
objectives: Define functions with def and explain the difference between parameters and arguments.
Use positional, keyword and default arguments, and avoid the mutable default trap.
Accept a variable number of arguments with *args and **kwargs and unpack them when calling.
Mark positional-only and keyword-only parameters with / and *.
Explain why a function without return returns None and how to return several values.
lesson.definition: A function is a named block of code that performs a task and can be called repeatedly with different inputs. A parameter is a name listed in the function definition; an argument is the actual object supplied at the call site. Parameters can be positional, keyword, defaulted, collected into *args and **kwargs, or restricted to positional-only or keyword-only, and a function may return one value, several values packed in a tuple, or None.

theory.heading: Defining and calling functions
theory.body: A def statement binds a function object to a name. Calling the name runs the body in a fresh local namespace; parameters are assigned from the arguments first. When the body finishes, control returns to the caller. If a function never executes a return statement it returns None, so functions used only for their side effects are called procedures. Docstrings are string literals placed first in the body; they are stored in __doc__ and are what help() displays. Reusing a function removes duplication and gives the logic a name, which is the reason the DRY principle exists.
points: def name(parameters): introduces a function; the body is indented.
Calling without arguments uses defaults or raises TypeError if a required one is missing.
No return statement means the function returns None.
return exits the function immediately and can return several values as a tuple.

theory.heading: Positional, keyword and default arguments
theory.body: Arguments are matched to parameters by position unless you write name=value at the call site, which binds by name. A parameter with a default value becomes optional, but the default expression is evaluated only once, when the def statement runs. That is why def append_to(item, box=[]) is a classic bug: every call shares the same list. Use an immutable sentinel such as None and create the mutable object inside the body instead. Required parameters must be written before defaulted ones.
points: f(1, 2) binds positionally; f(x=1, y=2) binds by name.
Never use a mutable default such as [] or {}; default to None and build inside.
Readable call sites use keyword arguments for booleans and options.
A parameter can become required two ways: no default, or keyword-only.

theory.heading: Variable arguments: *args and **kwargs
theory.body: A parameter written *args collects any extra positional arguments into a tuple, and **kwargs collects any extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. They let a function forward arguments it does not understand, which is essential for decorators and wrappers. At the call site the same symbols unpack in the other direction: f(*items) spreads a list or tuple into positional arguments and f(**mapping) spreads a dictionary into keyword arguments. The names args and kwargs are a convention; only the stars are required.
points: *args is a tuple of extra positional arguments.
**kwargs is a dict of extra keyword arguments.
f(*seq) and f(**d) unpack when calling.
A bare * in the parameter list makes the following parameters keyword-only.

theory.heading: Positional-only and keyword-only parameters
theory.body: A / in the parameter list marks the parameters before it as positional-only, so they cannot be passed by name. A plain * marks the parameters after it as keyword-only, so they must be passed by name. These markers make APIs explicit and stable: positional-only names can be renamed without breaking callers, and keyword-only parameters document intent and prevent confusing calls such as f(True, False). Standard functions such as pow(x, y, /) and max(iterable, *, default=...) use them.
points: def f(a, b, /, c, *, d): a and b positional-only, d keyword-only.
/ and * can be combined in one signature.
Keyword-only parameters are forced to be self-documenting.
The empty parameter list f() is not the same as the keyword-only marker *.

theory.heading: Functions are objects
theory.body: In Python a function is a first-class object: it can be stored in a variable, put in a list or dictionary, passed to another function and returned from one. That enables callbacks, sorting by a key function, and higher-order functions such as map, filter and functools.reduce. Aim for pure functions where possible: given the same arguments they return the same result and change nothing outside themselves, which makes them easy to test. Keep side effects deliberate and documented so callers are never surprised.
points: sorted(data, key=str.lower) passes a function as the key.
Functions have attributes such as __name__, __doc__ and __defaults__.
Pure functions are easier to test and reason about.
Closures and decorators build on functions being values.

example.title: The mutable default pitfall
example.body: The first version shares one list between all calls because the default is created once. The corrected version uses None as a sentinel and builds a fresh list on every call, which is the safe pattern.

code.source:
def buggy(item, box=[]):
    box.append(item)
    return box

print(buggy('a'))    # ['a']
print(buggy('b'))    # ['a', 'b']  shared list!

def fixed(item, box=None):
    if box is None:
        box = []
    box.append(item)
    return box

print(fixed('a'))    # ['a']
print(fixed('b'))    # ['b']  fresh list

use_cases.description: Passing functions to event handlers, sort keys and web framework route handlers.

takeaways: Parameters are the names in the definition; arguments are the values you pass.
Defaults are evaluated once at definition time, so never default to a mutable object.
Use None as a sentinel and create the list or dict inside the function.
*args collects extra positional arguments and **kwargs extra keyword arguments.
A function without return returns None; multiple return values arrive as a tuple.
Functions are objects, so they can be passed around as callbacks and keys.

interview.question: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
interview.answer: A parameter is the placeholder name in the function definition; an argument is the actual value passed when the function is called. Parameters are bound to the argument objects at call time.
interview.explanation: This sounds trivial but interviewers use it to check that you use precise vocabulary when discussing signatures.

interview.question: Why is def add_item(item, box=[]) dangerous?
interview.answer: Default values are evaluated once, when the def runs, so the same list object is reused by every call and items accumulate across unrelated calls. Default to None and create the list inside the function instead.
interview.explanation: This is the classic mutable-default-argument question; showing the fix demonstrates real experience.

interview.question: How do *args and **kwargs work?
interview.answer: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. At the call site, * unpacks a sequence into positional arguments and ** unpacks a mapping into keyword arguments.
interview.explanation: Mention their role in writing decorators and wrappers that must forward unknown arguments unchanged.

interview.question: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
interview.answer: None. Falling off the end of a function is equivalent to returning None, so functions that only print or modify state still return None.
interview.explanation: A good follow-up answer notes that returning several values is really returning a tuple, which the caller can unpack.

interview.question: What do the / and * markers in a parameter list mean?
interview.answer: Parameters before / are positional-only and cannot be passed by name; parameters after a bare * are keyword-only and must be passed by name. They let library authors make APIs explicit and keep internal parameter names free to change.
interview.explanation: Mention built-in examples such as pow(x, y, /) and that keyword-only arguments prevent confusing positional boolean calls.

practice.title: Greatest common divisor and least common multiple
practice.objective: Implement Euclid's algorithm in a reusable helper function and call it from a loop.
practice.statement: Read N pairs of non-negative integers. For each pair print the greatest common divisor and the least common multiple on one line. Define a function gcd(a, b) using Euclid's algorithm, and derive lcm(a, b) from it as a // gcd(a, b) * b, guarding the case where both numbers are zero.
practice.input_format: The first line is N. Each of the next N lines holds two non-negative integers a and b.
constraints: Define gcd as a function and reuse it inside lcm.
The least common multiple of two zeros is 0.
explanation: Euclid's algorithm replaces (a, b) with (b, a % b) until the remainder is 0; the last non-zero value is the gcd.
The assignment a, b = b, a % b uses tuple packing to read the old values before rebinding, so no temporary is needed.
Because a * b equals gcd * lcm, the lcm can be computed as a // gcd(a, b) * b; dividing before multiplying keeps the intermediate value small.
Both numbers zero is a special case, since dividing by a zero gcd would raise ZeroDivisionError.

print(add_item(1))

lesson.title: Scope, Namespaces and Closures
objectives: Explain the LEGB rule for resolving names: local, enclosing, global and built-in.
Use global and nonlocal to rebind names in outer scopes and explain why it is usually avoided.
Describe how a closure captures free variables and keeps them alive after the outer call returns.
Demonstrate late binding of a loop variable inside closures and apply the default-argument fix.
Diagnose UnboundLocalError from the rule that assignment makes a name local for the whole function.
lesson.definition: A namespace is a mapping from names to objects; a scope is the region of code where a name is visible. When Python resolves a name it searches, in order, the local scope, any enclosing function scopes, the module global scope and finally the built-ins. The global and nonlocal statements let a function rebind a name in an outer namespace instead of creating a new local one, and a nested function that references a variable from its enclosing scope forms a closure.

theory.heading: Namespaces and the LEGB rule
theory.body: Every module has a global namespace, every function call has a local namespace, and each block does not create a new scope, which is why variables assigned inside an if or for stay in the surrounding function. Name resolution follows LEGB: Local, then Enclosing function scopes from the inside out, then Global (the module), then Built-in. A name is looked up each time it is used, not bound in advance, so a function sees the current value of a global at call time. Shadowing happens when a local name hides one in an outer scope.
points: Local -> enclosing -> global -> built-in, checked in that order.
if, for and while do not create a new scope in Python.
globals() and locals() expose the current namespaces as dictionaries.
Shadowing is legal but can confuse readers; choose distinct names.

theory.heading: global and nonlocal
theory.body: By default, assigning to a name inside a function makes that name local for the entire function, even before the assignment line. The global statement tells Python that the name refers to the module namespace, and nonlocal tells it to refer to the nearest enclosing function scope. Reading a global needs no declaration; only rebinding does. Both should be used sparingly because they hide data flow and make functions hard to test. Passing values in as arguments and returning results out is almost always clearer.
points: global counter makes counter refer to the module-level variable.
nonlocal total rebinds total in the nearest enclosing function.
Reading globals is fine; rebinding triggers the need for global.
Prefer arguments and return values over hidden shared state.

theory.heading: Closures and free variables
theory.body: A closure is a nested function that refers to variables from its enclosing function. Those variables, called free variables, are captured in a cell object and kept alive even after the outer function returns. Closures are the mechanism behind decorators, callbacks and factory functions that produce configured behaviour. As long as the inner function exists, the captured objects are reachable, so they are not garbage collected. Python shows the captured names in the inner function's __closure__ and code.co_freevars attributes.
points: A closure keeps its enclosing variables alive after the outer call ends.
nonlocal lets the inner function assign to a captured variable.
Factory functions use closures to bake in configuration.
Decorators rely on closures to wrap a function with extra behaviour.

theory.heading: Late binding and the default-argument idiom
theory.body: Names inside a function body are looked up when the function runs, not when it is defined. In a loop that creates several lambdas or inner functions sharing one variable, they all see the final value of that variable, because they capture the variable rather than its value at creation time. This is called late binding. The fix is to give each function its own binding by capturing the value as a default argument, for example [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)], or to use functools.partial.
points: [lambda: i for i in range(3)] makes three closures all returning the final i.
[lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)] captures the current value.
functools.partial(func, i) binds arguments eagerly.
The same applies to functools.partial used as a callback factory.

theory.heading: Common pitfalls and recursion
theory.body: UnboundLocalError appears when a function assigns to a name and then reads it before that assignment, because the name is considered local throughout the function. NameError appears when no scope contains the name at all. Rebinding a global inside a function without declaring it creates a separate local, which is a frequent bug. Functions can call themselves, which is recursion; Python has a default recursion limit of about 1000 frames, and deep recursion can raise RecursionError, so iterative solutions may be preferable for large inputs.
points: Assignment anywhere in a function makes the name local everywhere in it.
Declare global or nonlocal before any use of the name.
sys.setrecursionlimit only raises the limit; it does not add stack memory.
Convert deep recursion to iteration to avoid RecursionError.

example.title: A closure-based counter
example.body: make_counter returns an inner function that remembers its own count. nonlocal lets that inner function rebind value in the enclosing scope instead of creating a local copy, so each counter keeps independent state.

code.source:
def make_counter(start=0):
    value = start
    def step():
        nonlocal value
        value += 1
        return value
    return step

c1 = make_counter()
c2 = make_counter(10)
print(c1(), c1(), c2())   # 1 2 11
print(c1())               # 3
print(c1.__closure__[0].cell_contents)  # 3

funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in funcs])          # [2, 2, 2] late binding

fixed = [lambda i=i: i for i in range(3)]
print([f() for f in fixed])          # [0, 1, 2]

def running_total():
    total = 0
    def add(n):
        nonlocal total
        total += n
        return total
    return add

add = running_total()
print(add(5), add(10), add(-3))      # 5 15 12

takeaways: Python resolves names with the LEGB rule: local, enclosing, global, built-in.
Assigning to a name anywhere in a function makes it local for the whole function.
global rebinds a module name; nonlocal rebinds a name in the nearest enclosing function.
A closure captures free variables and keeps them alive after the outer function returns.
Functions capture variables, not their values, which causes late binding in loops.
Capture a loop value with a default argument (lambda i=i: ...) to avoid late binding.

interview.question: What is the LEGB rule?
interview.answer: It is the order Python searches for a name: Local, then Enclosing function scopes, then Global (module) names, then Built-in names. The first scope that contains the name wins.
interview.explanation: Note that if, for and while bodies do not introduce a new scope, so their variables live in the enclosing function.

interview.question: When do you need the global and nonlocal keywords?
interview.answer: global is needed when a function assigns to a module-level name; nonlocal is needed when a nested function assigns to a variable in an enclosing function. Reading without assigning needs neither.
interview.explanation: A strong answer adds that both hide data flow, so arguments and return values are usually the better design.

interview.question: What is a closure?
interview.answer: A closure is a nested function that references variables from its enclosing function. Those free variables are captured in cell objects and remain available after the outer function returns, which is how counters and decorators keep state.
interview.explanation: You can inspect closures with func.__closure__ and func.__code__.co_freevars.

interview.question: Why do list comprehensions of lambdas all return the last value?
interview.answer: Because the lambdas capture the loop variable itself, not its value at each iteration, and the value is looked up when the lambda is called, after the loop has finished. Capture the current value with a default argument, as in lambda i=i: i.
interview.explanation: This late-binding behaviour is a favourite follow-up in interviews about closures and callbacks.

interview.question: What causes UnboundLocalError inside a function?
interview.answer: If a name is assigned anywhere in a function, Python treats it as local for the whole function. Reading it before the assignment line raises UnboundLocalError, even if a global with the same name exists.
interview.explanation: The fix is to declare global or nonlocal, or better, pass the value in as a parameter.

practice.title: Stateful command processor
practice.objective: Build a small state machine driven by commands, using a closure to hold state between calls.
practice.statement: Start from an initial value. Then process N commands in order: 'ADD k' adds k, 'SUB k' subtracts k, 'MUL k' multiplies by k, and 'RESET' returns the value to the initial one. Print the value after each command on its own line. Implement the mutable state inside a factory function using a nested function and nonlocal so the state stays private.
practice.input_format: The first line is the initial integer. The second line is N. Each of the next N lines is a command: 'ADD k', 'SUB k', 'MUL k' or 'RESET'.
practice.output_format: N lines, one value per command after it is applied.
constraints: -10^9 <= initial value and k <= 10^9.
RESET takes no argument.
Keep the running value in a closure using nonlocal.
practice.starter:
def make_processor(start):
    value = start
    def apply(command):
        nonlocal value
        # TODO: update value from the command and return it
        return value
    return apply

start = int(input())
n = int(input())
apply = make_processor(start)
for _ in range(n):
    print(apply(input().strip()))
explanation: make_processor keeps start and value in its own namespace; the returned apply function is a closure over both.
nonlocal lets the inner function rebind value in the enclosing scope instead of shadowing it with a new local name.
Each command is split into an operation and an optional argument, so RESET simply has one part.
On RESET the closure restores value from the captured start variable.

quiz.question: Which order does Python use to resolve a name?
quiz.explanation: The LEGB rule checks the local scope, then enclosing function scopes, then module globals, then built-ins.

x = 10
def f():
    x = 20
    return x
print(f(), x)
quiz.explanation: The assignment inside f makes x local to f, so f returns 20 while the module-level x stays 10.

quiz.question: When is the nonlocal keyword required?
options: To declare a variable as a constant
To import a name from another module
To reassign a variable defined in an enclosing function from a nested function
To read a global variable inside a function
quiz.explanation: nonlocal binds the name to the nearest enclosing function scope so the inner function can rebind it.
