quiz.code:
funcs = [lambda: i for i in range(3)]
print(funcs[0](), funcs[2]())
quiz.explanation: Each lambda captures the variable i, not its value, so after the loop both calls see the final value 2.

quiz.question: Inside a function you write total += 1, where total is a module-level name, and the call raises UnboundLocalError. What is the cause?
options: Module-level names are never visible inside functions.
Because total is assigned somewhere in the function, Python treats it as local for the whole function.
total is read-only at module level.
The += operator cannot be used with names from other scopes.
quiz.explanation: Assignment makes a name local for the entire function, so reading it before rebinding raises UnboundLocalError; declare global or pass the value in.

questions.topic: Python Overview and the Execution Model
questions.question: Is Python a compiled or an interpreted language?
questions.answer: Both, in the CPython implementation. Source code is compiled to bytecode, and the bytecode is executed by the Python Virtual Machine, an interpreter. It is not compiled ahead of time to native machine code.
questions.explanation: Saying only 'interpreted' is the common weak answer. A strong answer names the pipeline (source -> AST -> bytecode -> PVM) and mentions that PyPy adds JIT compilation.

questions.topic: Python Overview and the Execution Model
questions.question: What is the purpose of if __name__ == '__main__':?
questions.answer: It runs the guarded block only when the file is executed directly. When the file is imported, __name__ is the module name, so the block is skipped and importing has no side effects.
questions.explanation: Mention practical uses: CLI entry points, quick demos and avoiding duplicate work when multiprocessing re-imports the main module on Windows.

questions.topic: Python Overview and the Execution Model
questions.question: What are .pyc files and __pycache__?
questions.answer: .pyc files hold the compiled bytecode of imported modules, stored in __pycache__ with a version tag. Python reuses them when the source is unchanged, which speeds up imports. They do not make code run faster once loaded.
questions.explanation: Interviewers check that you know caching affects start-up time only, and that the main script is not cached.

questions.topic: Python Overview and the Execution Model
questions.question: A file has a syntax error on its last line. Does the first print statement run?
questions.answer: No. The whole file is parsed and compiled before execution starts, so the SyntaxError is raised before any statement runs. A NameError on the last line, by contrast, would only occur after the earlier lines had executed.
questions.explanation: This tests real understanding of the execution model: compile-time versus run-time errors.

questions.topic: Python Overview and the Execution Model
questions.question: What are the main limitations of Python, and how do teams work around them?
questions.answer: CPU-bound code is slower than in compiled languages, the GIL stops threads running Python bytecode in parallel, objects use more memory and type errors surface at run time. Teams use C-backed libraries (NumPy), multiprocessing or native extensions for speed, PyPy for some workloads, and type hints with mypy plus tests for correctness.
questions.explanation: Balanced answers that pair each limitation with a mitigation sound like real engineering experience.

questions.topic: Variables, Dynamic Typing and Object References
questions.question: What does it mean that Python is dynamically typed?
questions.answer: Types are attached to objects rather than variables and are checked at run time. A name can refer to an int and later to a str, and you never declare types.
questions.explanation: Add that Python is still strongly typed ('3' + 4 raises TypeError) to stand out.

questions.topic: Variables, Dynamic Typing and Object References
questions.question: What is the difference between == and is?
questions.answer: == checks whether two objects have equal values (via __eq__). is checks whether two names refer to the same object in memory. Use is for None and other singletons.
questions.explanation: Give the list example: [1] == [1] is True, [1] is [1] is False.

questions.topic: Variables, Dynamic Typing and Object References
questions.question: Why might a = 256; b = 256; a is b be True but the same test with 257 be False?
questions.answer: CPython caches small integers from -5 to 256, so both names get the same cached object. Larger integers may be created separately, so identity is not guaranteed. This is an implementation detail, and numbers should always be compared with ==.
questions.explanation: Interviewers want you to know the reason and the lesson: never rely on is for value comparison.

questions.topic: Variables, Dynamic Typing and Object References
questions.question: After a = [1, 2]; b = a; b += [3], what is a? What if the lists were tuples?
questions.answer: a is [1, 2, 3] because += on a list mutates it in place and both names share it. With tuples, b += (3,) creates a new tuple and rebinds b, so a stays (1, 2).
questions.explanation: This shows you understand that += calls __iadd__ when available (mutable types) and falls back to creating a new object for immutable types.

questions.topic: Variables, Dynamic Typing and Object References
questions.question: Are type hints enforced at run time? Why use them?
questions.answer: No. The interpreter stores them in __annotations__ but does not check them. They are used by static checkers (mypy, pyright), IDEs and frameworks such as FastAPI and pydantic, which read them deliberately to validate data.
questions.explanation: Mentioning that some libraries opt in to run-time validation shows current, practical knowledge.

questions.topic: Numbers and Strings: Slicing, Formatting and Methods
questions.question: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 not equal 0.3 in Python?
questions.answer: Floats are stored in binary, and 0.1 and 0.2 have no exact binary representation, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with math.isclose, or use Decimal or integers for exact values.
questions.explanation: Mention that this is IEEE 754 behaviour shared by most languages, not a Python bug.

questions.topic: Numbers and Strings: Slicing, Formatting and Methods
questions.question: How do you reverse a string in Python?
questions.answer: Use slicing with a step of -1: s[::-1]. Alternatively ''.join(reversed(s)).
questions.explanation: Interviewers often follow up with a palindrome check: s == s[::-1], possibly after normalising case and removing non-alphanumeric characters.

questions.topic: Numbers and Strings: Slicing, Formatting and Methods
questions.question: Why are strings immutable, and what are the consequences?
questions.answer: Immutability lets strings be hashed and used as dict keys and set members, makes them safe to share between names and threads, and enables interning. The consequence is that every modification creates a new string, so repeated += in a loop is inefficient compared with ''.join.
questions.explanation: Linking immutability to hashability and performance shows depth.

questions.topic: Numbers and Strings: Slicing, Formatting and Methods
questions.question: What is the difference between str.find and str.index?
questions.answer: Both return the lowest index of a substring. find returns -1 when it is not found; index raises ValueError.
questions.explanation: Choose find when absence is normal, index when absence is an error you want surfaced.

questions.topic: Numbers and Strings: Slicing, Formatting and Methods
questions.question: What does round(2.5) return, and why?
questions.answer: 2. Python 3 uses round half to even (banker's rounding), so .5 cases round to the nearest even number. This reduces bias when many values are rounded. For commercial rounding use Decimal.quantize with ROUND_HALF_UP.
questions.explanation: A surprising-output question that tests attention to numeric details.

questions.topic: Operators, Expressions and Precedence
questions.question: What is the difference between / and // in Python 3?
questions.answer: / is true division and always returns a float. // is floor division: it rounds the result down toward negative infinity, returning an int for int operands, so -7 // 2 is -4.
questions.explanation: Mentioning the negative-number behaviour separates a strong answer from a memorised one.

questions.topic: Operators, Expressions and Precedence
questions.question: What does 'a or b' return?
questions.answer: It returns a if a is truthy, otherwise b. It does not convert the result to a bool, and b is not evaluated when a is truthy.
questions.explanation: Link it to idioms such as name = value or 'default', and warn that 0 or '' are also replaced, which may be unintended.

questions.topic: Operators, Expressions and Precedence
questions.question: How do you check whether a number is a power of two without loops?
questions.answer: n > 0 and n & (n - 1) == 0. A power of two has exactly one set bit, and subtracting 1 flips that bit and all lower bits, so the AND is zero.
questions.explanation: Explaining why the trick works is more important than the formula itself.

questions.topic: Operators, Expressions and Precedence
questions.question: What does 1 < 3 > 2 evaluate to, and why?
questions.answer: True. Python chains comparisons, so it means 1 < 3 and 3 > 2, both of which are true.
questions.explanation: Shows you know chaining is a language feature, not left-to-right evaluation of booleans.

questions.topic: Operators, Expressions and Precedence
questions.question: What is the walrus operator and when would you use it?
questions.answer: The assignment expression := (Python 3.8) binds a name as part of an expression. It avoids repeating a computation, for example while (chunk := f.read(1024)): process(chunk) or [y for x in data if (y := f(x)) > 0].
questions.explanation: Mention it should be used where it improves clarity, not to cram logic into one line.

questions.topic: Control Flow: Conditionals, Loops and Loop Control
questions.question: What is the difference between break and continue?
questions.answer: break exits the innermost loop immediately. continue skips the remaining statements of the current iteration and moves straight to the next pass, where the loop condition is tested again.
questions.explanation: Mention that neither statement affects an outer loop, which is a common follow-up question about nested loops.

questions.topic: Control Flow: Conditionals, Loops and Loop Control
questions.question: What does the else clause on a for or while loop do?
questions.answer: It runs after the loop finishes normally, meaning only if the loop was not exited with break. It is typically used to handle the not-found case of a search without a flag variable.
questions.explanation: A strong answer contrasts it with the if/else else and gives a search example such as for/else over a list of records.

questions.topic: Control Flow: Conditionals, Loops and Loop Control
questions.question: How do you loop with an index in Python, and why avoid range(len(items))?
questions.answer: Use for i, item in enumerate(items). range(len(items)) works but is less readable and error-prone because you index the sequence yourself and lose the direct reference to the item.
questions.explanation: enumerate also accepts a start value, which is handy for numbering lines starting at one.

questions.topic: Control Flow: Conditionals, Loops and Loop Control
questions.question: Why does deleting items from a list while looping over it skip elements?
questions.answer: Removing an element shifts every later element one position left, but the iterator's internal index still moves forward, so the element that slid into the current position is never visited. Iterate over a copy, delete in reverse, or build a new list instead.
questions.explanation: The same class of bug affects any sequence whose length changes during iteration.

questions.topic: Control Flow: Conditionals, Loops and Loop Control
questions.question: When would you choose while over for?
questions.answer: When the number of iterations is not known in advance, for example reading until a sentinel value, retrying an operation until it succeeds, or advancing a value until some condition holds. for is preferable whenever you are walking over the items of an iterable.
questions.explanation: Interviewers like to hear that for loops are implemented on top of the iterator protocol and handling IndexError manually is not idiomatic.

questions.topic: Functions: Parameters, Arguments and Return Values
questions.question: What is the difference between a parameter and an argument?
questions.answer: A parameter is the placeholder name in the function definition; an argument is the actual value passed when the function is called. Parameters are bound to the argument objects at call time.
questions.explanation: This sounds trivial but interviewers use it to check that you use precise vocabulary when discussing signatures.

questions.topic: Functions: Parameters, Arguments and Return Values
questions.question: Why is def add_item(item, box=[]) dangerous?
questions.answer: Default values are evaluated once, when the def runs, so the same list object is reused by every call and items accumulate across unrelated calls. Default to None and create the list inside the function instead.
questions.explanation: This is the classic mutable-default-argument question; showing the fix demonstrates real experience.

questions.topic: Functions: Parameters, Arguments and Return Values
questions.question: How do *args and **kwargs work?
questions.answer: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dictionary. At the call site, * unpacks a sequence into positional arguments and ** unpacks a mapping into keyword arguments.
questions.explanation: Mention their role in writing decorators and wrappers that must forward unknown arguments unchanged.

questions.topic: Functions: Parameters, Arguments and Return Values
questions.question: What does a function return if it has no return statement?
questions.answer: None. Falling off the end of a function is equivalent to returning None, so functions that only print or modify state still return None.
questions.explanation: A good follow-up answer notes that returning several values is really returning a tuple, which the caller can unpack.

questions.topic: Functions: Parameters, Arguments and Return Values
questions.question: What do the / and * markers in a parameter list mean?
questions.answer: Parameters before / are positional-only and cannot be passed by name; parameters after a bare * are keyword-only and must be passed by name. They let library authors make APIs explicit and keep internal parameter names free to change.
questions.explanation: Mention built-in examples such as pow(x, y, /) and that keyword-only arguments prevent confusing positional boolean calls.

questions.topic: Scope, Namespaces and Closures
questions.question: What is the LEGB rule?
questions.answer: It is the order Python searches for a name: Local, then Enclosing function scopes, then Global (module) names, then Built-in names. The first scope that contains the name wins.
questions.explanation: Note that if, for and while bodies do not introduce a new scope, so their variables live in the enclosing function.

questions.topic: Scope, Namespaces and Closures
questions.question: When do you need the global and nonlocal keywords?
questions.answer: global is needed when a function assigns to a module-level name; nonlocal is needed when a nested function assigns to a variable in an enclosing function. Reading without assigning needs neither.
questions.explanation: A strong answer adds that both hide data flow, so arguments and return values are usually the better design.

questions.topic: Scope, Namespaces and Closures
questions.question: What is a closure?
questions.answer: A closure is a nested function that references variables from its enclosing function. Those free variables are captured in cell objects and remain available after the outer function returns, which is how counters and decorators keep state.
questions.explanation: You can inspect closures with func.__closure__ and func.__code__.co_freevars.

questions.topic: Scope, Namespaces and Closures
questions.question: Why do list comprehensions of lambdas all return the last value?
questions.answer: Because the lambdas capture the loop variable itself, not its value at each iteration, and the value is looked up when the lambda is called, after the loop has finished. Capture the current value with a default argument, as in lambda i=i: i.
questions.explanation: This late-binding behaviour is a favourite follow-up in interviews about closures and callbacks.

questions.topic: Scope, Namespaces and Closures
questions.question: What causes UnboundLocalError inside a function?
questions.answer: If a name is assigned anywhere in a function, Python treats it as local for the whole function. Reading it before the assignment line raises UnboundLocalError, even if a global with the same name exists.
questions.explanation: The fix is to declare global or nonlocal, or better, pass the value in as a parameter.

days.title: Python Overview and the Execution Model
days.focus: Python is a high-level, general-purpose, dynamically typed programming language that emphasises readability. The standard implementation, CPython, first compiles a source file into bytecode (a low-level, platform-independent instruction set) and then executes that bytecode on the Python Virtual Machine, an interpreter loop written in C.
objectives: Describe what Python is and why it is popular for back-end, automation and data work.
Explain how CPython compiles source code to bytecode and runs it on a virtual machine.
Distinguish compile-time errors (SyntaxError) from run-time errors (NameError, TypeError).
Explain the role of __name__ == '__main__' and .pyc caching.
Answer the classic 'Is Python compiled or interpreted?' interview question precisely.
days.assignment: Read a small Python program and report whether it compiles. Do not execute it. If it compiles, print OK followed by the number of non-blank lines. If it does not, print the line number of the syntax error reported by the compiler. IndentationError is a kind of SyntaxError and must be reported the same way.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: CPython compiles source to bytecode, then the Python Virtual Machine interprets the bytecode.
A SyntaxError anywhere in a file prevents any of it from running; NameError and TypeError appear only when the line executes.
.pyc files in __pycache__ cache bytecode of imported modules to speed up start-up.
if __name__ == '__main__': separates script behaviour from importable code.
Python trades raw CPU speed for readability and productivity; heavy lifting is delegated to C extensions.
CPython, PyPy, Jython and MicroPython are different implementations of the same language.

days.title: Variables, Dynamic Typing and Object References
days.focus: In Python a variable is a name that refers to an object stored in memory. Assignment binds a name to an object; it never copies the object. Python is dynamically typed, meaning the type belongs to the object and is checked at run time, so the same name can refer to an int now and a string later.
objectives: Explain that Python variables are names bound to objects, not boxes holding values.
Contrast dynamic typing with static typing and strong typing with weak typing.
Use id(), type(), isinstance(), == and is correctly.
Predict the effect of assignment, rebinding and in-place mutation on shared objects.
Recognise interning and small-integer caching as implementation details.
days.assignment: Each input line contains one Python literal. For each line print the name of its type and whether that type is mutable or immutable. Parse literals safely with ast.literal_eval instead of eval. Treat list, dict and set as mutable; every other type produced by a literal is immutable.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: Variables are names bound to objects; assignment never copies.
Python is dynamically and strongly typed.
== compares values; is compares identity. Use is only with None, True and False.
Mutating a shared object is visible through every name that refers to it; rebinding is not.
Small-integer caching and string interning are CPython optimisations, not guarantees.
Type hints are documentation for tools; the interpreter does not enforce them.

days.title: Numbers and Strings: Slicing, Formatting and Methods
days.focus: Python's numeric types are int (arbitrary precision integers), float (64-bit IEEE 754 binary floating point) and complex, with Decimal and Fraction available in the standard library for exact arithmetic. A str is an immutable sequence of Unicode characters that supports indexing, slicing, a rich set of methods and formatted string literals (f-strings).
objectives: Use int, float, complex and Decimal appropriately and explain floating-point error.
Slice strings with start, stop and step, including negative indices.
Format output with f-strings and format specifiers.
Apply common string methods: split, join, strip, replace, find, startswith, upper and title.
Explain why strings are immutable and why ''.join is preferred over += in loops.

For each line print the item name with underscores replaced by spaces in title case, left-aligned in 14 characters, then the quantity right-aligned in 4 characters, then the line amount right-aligned in 10 characters with exactly two decimals. Finally print TOTAL left-aligned in 18 characters followed by the grand total right-aligned in 10 characters. To avoid floating-point error, convert prices to integer paise before multiplying.

Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: ints have unlimited precision; floats are approximate, so compare them with math.isclose.
Use integer paise/cents or Decimal for money.
Slices exclude the stop index, accept negative indices and never raise IndexError.
Strings are immutable; methods return new strings.
Join many pieces with ''.join(list) instead of += in a loop.
f-strings with format specifiers handle alignment, decimals and separators.

days.title: Operators, Expressions and Precedence
days.focus: An operator is a symbol or keyword that combines values (operands) into an expression that Python evaluates to a single object. Python groups operators into arithmetic, comparison, logical, bitwise, identity, membership and assignment operators, and evaluates them according to fixed precedence and associativity rules.
objectives: Use arithmetic operators correctly, including floor division and modulo with negative numbers.
Explain short-circuit evaluation and why and/or return operands rather than booleans.
Read chained comparisons and operator precedence without guessing.
Apply bitwise operators to classic interview tasks.
Use the walrus operator := and augmented assignment appropriately.
days.assignment: For each non-negative integer, print: the number, its binary representation without the 0b prefix, the count of 1 bits, 'yes' or 'no' for whether it is a power of two (using n & (n - 1)), and 'even' or 'odd' decided with n & 1.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: / always returns a float; // floors toward negative infinity.
% takes the sign of the divisor, so it wraps negative indices cleanly.
** is right-associative and binds tighter than unary minus.
and/or short-circuit and return one of their operands, not necessarily a bool.
n & (n - 1) == 0 (with n > 0) detects powers of two.
Use parentheses whenever precedence is not obvious to a reader.

days.title: Control Flow: Conditionals, Loops and Loop Control
days.focus: Control flow is the order in which a program's statements run. Python selects a branch with the conditional statement if/elif/else, which tests truthiness, and repeats work with two loops: for, which visits each item of an iterable in turn, and while, which repeats as long as a condition stays true. break, continue and the optional else clause attached to a loop give fine-grained control over how iteration ends.
objectives: Write if/elif/else chains that choose between mutually exclusive branches.
Iterate over sequences and ranges with for loops and use while for sentinel-driven repetition.
Use break, continue and the loop else clause to control iteration precisely.
Explain when the else attached to a loop runs and why it pairs with break.
Recognise pitfalls such as mutating a list while iterating over it.
days.assignment: The Collatz process maps an even number n to n / 2 and an odd number n to 3 * n + 1, repeating until n reaches 1. For each starting value print the starting value and the number of steps needed to reach 1. A starting value of 1 takes zero steps.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: if/elif/else selects exactly one branch; truthiness avoids comparisons with True.
Use for over iterables and while when the number of iterations is unknown.
break stops the innermost loop; continue skips to the next pass.
A loop else runs only when no break occurred, making it ideal for searches.
Never mutate a list while iterating it; iterate over a copy or build a new list.

days.title: Functions: Parameters, Arguments and Return Values
days.focus: A function is a named block of code that performs a task and can be called repeatedly with different inputs. A parameter is a name listed in the function definition; an argument is the actual object supplied at the call site. Parameters can be positional, keyword, defaulted, collected into *args and **kwargs, or restricted to positional-only or keyword-only, and a function may return one value, several values packed in a tuple, or None.
objectives: Define functions with def and explain the difference between parameters and arguments.
Use positional, keyword and default arguments, and avoid the mutable default trap.
Accept a variable number of arguments with *args and **kwargs and unpack them when calling.
Mark positional-only and keyword-only parameters with / and *.
Explain why a function without return returns None and how to return several values.
days.assignment: Read N pairs of non-negative integers. For each pair print the greatest common divisor and the least common multiple on one line. Define a function gcd(a, b) using Euclid's algorithm, and derive lcm(a, b) from it as a // gcd(a, b) * b, guarding the case where both numbers are zero.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: Parameters are the names in the definition; arguments are the values you pass.
Defaults are evaluated once at definition time, so never default to a mutable object.
Use None as a sentinel and create the list or dict inside the function.
*args collects extra positional arguments and **kwargs extra keyword arguments.
A function without return returns None; multiple return values arrive as a tuple.
Functions are objects, so they can be passed around as callbacks and keys.

days.title: Scope, Namespaces and Closures
days.focus: A namespace is a mapping from names to objects; a scope is the region of code where a name is visible. When Python resolves a name it searches, in order, the local scope, any enclosing function scopes, the module global scope and finally the built-ins. The global and nonlocal statements let a function rebind a name in an outer namespace instead of creating a new local one, and a nested function that references a variable from its enclosing scope forms a closure.
objectives: Explain the LEGB rule for resolving names: local, enclosing, global and built-in.
Use global and nonlocal to rebind names in outer scopes and explain why it is usually avoided.
Describe how a closure captures free variables and keeps them alive after the outer call returns.
Demonstrate late binding of a loop variable inside closures and apply the default-argument fix.
Diagnose UnboundLocalError from the rule that assignment makes a name local for the whole function.
days.assignment: Start from an initial value. Then process N commands in order: 'ADD k' adds k, 'SUB k' subtracts k, 'MUL k' multiplies by k, and 'RESET' returns the value to the initial one. Print the value after each command on its own line. Implement the mutable state inside a factory function using a nested function and nonlocal so the state stays private.
steps: Read the concept and work through the example
Implement the practice task without opening the solution
Run the provided cases and add an edge case
Explain your result and complete the revision checklist
revision: Python resolves names with the LEGB rule: local, enclosing, global, built-in.
Assigning to a name anywhere in a function makes it local for the whole function.
global rebinds a module name; nonlocal rebinds a name in the nearest enclosing function.
A closure captures free variables and keeps them alive after the outer function returns.
Functions capture variables, not their values, which causes late binding in loops.
Capture a loop value with a default argument (lambda i=i: ...) to avoid late binding.

lesson.title: Built-in Data Structures: Lists, Tuples, Sets and Dictionaries
objectives: Choose between list, tuple, set and dict based on ordering, mutability and lookup needs.
Use the core methods of lists and dictionaries confidently and correctly.
Explain hashing and why set and dict membership tests are O(1) on average.
Combine and compare collections with the set operations for union, intersection and difference.
Recognise when Counter and defaultdict replace hand-written bookkeeping.
lesson.definition: Python's four built-in collections cover most everyday needs. A list is an ordered, mutable sequence; a tuple is an ordered, immutable sequence that can be hashed and used as a dictionary key; a set is an unordered collection of unique hashable objects with fast membership tests; and a dict is a mapping of unique hashable keys to values that preserves insertion order. Each trades off ordering, mutability and lookup speed differently.

theory.heading: Lists: ordered and mutable
theory.body: A list stores references to objects in order and can grow or shrink. Indexing and slicing are fast, and append and pop at the end are amortised O(1), but inserting or deleting near the front is O(n) because it shifts every later element. Useful methods include append, extend, insert, remove, pop, index, count, sort, reverse and copy. Because a list holds references, a nested list can accidentally be shared; copying with [:] or list() is shallow, so use copy.deepcopy for nested mutable data.
points: append adds one item; extend adds every item of an iterable.
ls.sort() sorts in place and returns None; sorted(ls) returns a new list.
slicing ls[:] makes a shallow copy.
Membership on a list is O(n); on a set it is O(1).

theory.heading: Tuples: ordered and immutable
theory.body: A tuple is like a frozen list. It cannot be changed after creation, which makes it safe to share and allows it to be hashed, so tuples can be keys in a dict or members of a set, provided all their elements are hashable too. Tuples are the natural representation of a fixed record such as a coordinate or a database row, and returning several values from a function really returns a tuple. namedtuple from collections, or dataclasses, give those records named fields.
points: (1, 2) and 1, 2 both build a tuple; a one-element tuple needs a trailing comma: (1,).
Tuples are hashable if every element is hashable.
Packing and unpacking let you swap values: a, b = b, a.
namedtuple adds readable field names without losing tuple behaviour.

theory.heading: Sets: unique and fast to test
theory.body: A set keeps one copy of each hashable value and does not preserve order. Its power comes from O(1) average membership tests and from mathematical operations: | for union, & for intersection, - for difference and ^ for symmetric difference. Use a set to remove duplicates from a sequence with set(items) or to test whether two collections share values. A frozenset is an immutable, hashable set that can itself be used as a dictionary key. Sets cannot hold lists or dictionaries because those are unhashable.
points: {1, 2, 3} or set([1, 2, 3]) creates a set; {} creates an empty dict, not a set.
set(items) removes duplicates but loses order.
a & b, a | b, a - b, a ^ b perform the set operations.
add, discard, remove and issubset are common methods.

theory.heading: Dictionaries: key-value lookups
theory.body: A dict maps hashable keys to arbitrary values and, since Python 3.7, remembers insertion order. Lookups by key are O(1) on average. Reading a missing key with d[k] raises KeyError, while d.get(k) returns None and d.get(k, default) returns your fallback. Keys must be hashable, so use tuples or strings, not lists. Useful methods include keys, values, items, setdefault, update and pop. Comprehensions and Counter cover most counting and grouping tasks without extra loops.
points: d.get(k, default) avoids KeyError for missing keys.
d.items() yields (key, value) pairs for iteration.
Keys must be hashable; insertion order of keys is preserved.
Counter and defaultdict remove the need for manual default checks.

theory.heading: Choosing a structure and complexity
theory.body: Pick the structure from the operations you perform most. Need order and frequent appends: list. Need an immutable record or a hashable key: tuple. Need uniqueness or fast membership: set. Need to associate values with keys: dict. Remember the average costs: list indexing is O(1) but membership is O(n); set and dict membership is O(1) average; sorting anything is O(n log n). Converting between types is cheap enough, so it is normal to build a list, then a set to deduplicate, then back to a list when order matters.
points: list: ordered, mutable, O(n) search, O(1) index.
tuple: ordered, immutable, hashable, good as a key.
set: unordered, unique, O(1) average membership.
dict: keyed, ordered, O(1) average lookup.
List -> set -> sorted list is the usual deduplicate-and-order recipe.

example.title: Counting with a dictionary and Counter
example.body: A plain dictionary counts words with dict.get, while collections.Counter does the same job in fewer lines. Sorting the items by count turns the counts into a simple frequency report.

code.source:
from collections import Counter

words = 'the cat the hat the cat'.split()

counts = {}
for w in words:
    counts[w] = counts.get(w, 0) + 1
print(counts)

counter = Counter(words)
print(counter.most_common(2))
print(sorted(counts.items(), key=lambda kv: (-kv[1], kv[0])))

use_cases.description: list(set(items)) drops repeated values; pair it with sorted() to restore a stable order.

use_cases.title: Membership tests on large data
use_cases.description: Checking an allow-list with a set is far faster than scanning a list for every request.

use_cases.title: Grouping and tallying
use_cases.description: Dictionaries and Counter group records by key and count occurrences in one pass.

use_cases.title: Fixed records
use_cases.description: Tuples and namedtuples represent coordinates, rows and return values that must not change.

takeaways: list is ordered and mutable; tuple is ordered and immutable, so it can be a key.
set stores unique values and gives O(1) average membership and set operations.
dict maps hashable keys to values and preserves insertion order.
Reading a missing key with [] raises KeyError; get returns a default instead.
Keys of dicts and members of sets must be hashable, so lists cannot be used.
Counter and defaultdict replace repetitive counting and default-checking code.

interview.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
interview.answer: A list is mutable and typically holds homogeneous items you will change; a tuple is immutable, often holds a fixed record, and being hashable it can be a dictionary key or set member if its elements are hashable.
interview.explanation: Mention that immutability makes tuples safe to share and slightly cheaper to create, though speed is rarely the deciding factor.

interview.question: Why is checking membership in a set faster than in a list?
interview.answer: A set is built on a hash table, so membership computes the hash of the value and checks a bucket, which is O(1) on average. A list must compare against items one by one and is O(n).
interview.explanation: The same hashing explains fast dictionary key lookups; note that worst-case behaviour can degrade if hashes collide.

interview.question: Why can't a list be used as a dictionary key?
interview.answer: Dictionary keys must be hashable, and hashability requires an object whose hash never changes. A list can be mutated, so its hash could change and break the mapping. Use a tuple instead.
interview.explanation: This links to __hash__ and __eq__ being defined together; mutable containers deliberately set __hash__ to None.

interview.question: How do you remove duplicates from a list while keeping order?
interview.answer: Build a set for fast membership and collect items in a new list only the first time they appear, for example dict.fromkeys(items) in Python 3.7+, or a loop with a seen set. A plain set(items) removes duplicates but loses the original order.
interview.explanation: dict.fromkeys is a neat one-liner because dictionaries preserve insertion order and the keys are unique.

interview.question: What is the average time complexity of common operations on these structures?
interview.answer: List indexing is O(1), list search is O(n), and appending is amortised O(1). Set and dict membership, insertion and deletion are O(1) on average. Sorting any of them is O(n log n).
interview.explanation: Interviewers like candidates who can map a data structure choice to the expected complexity rather than guessing.

lesson.title: Strings, Formatting and Regular Expressions
objectives: Master the f-string and format mini-language for alignment, precision and custom formatting.
Use the re module for search, fullmatch, findall and sub on real text.
Build and explain patterns with character classes, quantifiers, anchors and groups.
Distinguish str from bytes and encode or decode text correctly.
Avoid catastrophic backtracking and prefer raw strings for patterns.
lesson.definition: Text data in Python is handled with the immutable str type, which stores Unicode code points and is formatted with f-strings and the format mini-language. Complex matching and transformation is done with the re module, whose patterns combine literal characters, character classes, quantifiers, anchors and groups. Bytes, a separate bytes type produced by encode, are used for raw binary data and decoded back to str with a chosen encoding such as UTF-8.

theory.heading: str and bytes
theory.body: A str is a sequence of Unicode code points; a bytes object is a sequence of raw bytes from 0 to 255. Text read from the network or a binary file is bytes and must be decoded with a character set, usually UTF-8, to become str. Writing with an unknown or wrong encoding produces mojibake or UnicodeDecodeError. Because characters can need several bytes, len(text) counts characters while len(text.encode('utf-8')) counts bytes, which is why limits are sometimes measured in bytes rather than characters.
points: str.encode('utf-8') turns text into bytes; bytes.decode('utf-8') turns bytes into text.
len of a str counts characters, len of bytes counts bytes.
The encoding is metadata; the same bytes can decode differently with the wrong codec.
Use errors='replace' only when you are willing to lose data.

theory.heading: Formatting in depth
theory.body: An f-string evaluates expressions inside braces and applies a format specifier after a colon. The mini-language composes an optional fill and alignment (< left, > right, ^ centre, = after the sign), a sign, a width, a grouping option and a precision with a type such as f for fixed point, e for scientific, d for integer or s for string. A comma adds thousands separators and a percent type multiplies by 100. Objects can customise their own rendering by defining __format__. str.format and the older percent style still appear in legacy code.
points: {value:>10.2f} right-aligns a float in width 10 with two decimals.
{value:^10} centres text in a field of 10.
{n:,} inserts thousands separators; {p:.1%} formats a fraction as a percentage.
{x=} prints the expression and its value, useful when debugging.

theory.heading: Regular expressions: searching and matching
theory.body: The re module compiles a pattern into a regular expression object whose methods scan text. re.search finds the first match anywhere, re.match anchors at the start, re.fullmatch requires the whole string to match, re.findall returns a list of all matches and re.finditer yields match objects with positions. re.sub replaces matches with a replacement string, which may reference captured groups. Compiling once with re.compile and reusing the object is faster when the same pattern is applied to many strings.
points: search looks anywhere; match anchors at the start; fullmatch requires the entire string.
findall returns strings; finditer returns match objects with .group() and .span().
sub(pattern, repl, text, count=0) replaces every match by default.
Compile a pattern once and reuse it in loops.

theory.heading: Pattern building blocks and groups
theory.body: Square brackets define a character class such as [abc] or a range [0-9], the dot matches any character except newline, and quantifiers control repetition: * zero or more, + one or more, ? zero or one and {m,n} between m and n. Quantifiers are greedy by default and consume as much as possible; adding ? makes them lazy. Anchors ^ and $ pin a match to the start and end, and backslash classes such as \d, \w and \s mean digit, word character and whitespace. Parentheses group parts of a pattern and capture them so they can be reused or extracted.
points: \d matches a digit, \w a letter, digit or underscore, \s whitespace.
+ is greedy, +? is lazy and matches as little as possible.
(...) captures a group; (?:...) groups without capturing.
(?P<name>...) names a group so it can be read by name.

theory.heading: Performance and pitfalls
theory.body: Patterns full of nested quantifiers such as (a+)+ can backtrack catastrophically and hang on long inputs; keep patterns specific and prefer simple string methods when they suffice. Always write patterns as raw strings, r'...', so backslashes reach the engine instead of being treated as escapes. Special characters such as . * + ? ( ) [ ] { } ^ $ | must be escaped with a backslash when you mean them literally. Beware that . does not match a newline unless the re.DOTALL flag is set, and that findall returns the groups, not the whole match, when the pattern contains capturing groups.
points: Use raw strings: r'\d+' not '\\d+'.
Avoid nested quantifiers that cause catastrophic backtracking.
Escape special characters when matching them literally.
Prefer str.split or str.startswith when no pattern is needed.

example.title: Extracting and rewriting with re
example.body: Named groups make an extracted date readable, and re.sub with a replacement template rewrites a messy version string into a clean one. The pattern is compiled once and reused.

code.source:
import re

log = '2024-06-01 INFO login ok, 2024-06-02 WARN disk 91%'
date = re.compile(r'(?P<year>\d{4})-(?P<month>\d{2})-(?P<day>\d{2})')
match = date.search(log)
print(match.group('day'), match.group('month'), match.group('year'))
print(date.findall(log))

messy = 'version 1-2-3 released'
print(re.sub(r'(\d+)-(\d+)-(\d+)', r'\1.\2.\3', messy))

interview.question: What is the difference between str and bytes in Python?
interview.answer: str is a sequence of Unicode characters used for text; bytes is a sequence of raw byte values used for binary data. You move between them with encode and decode using an encoding such as UTF-8, and mixing them raises TypeError.
interview.explanation: Mention that len differs because a character can need several bytes in UTF-8.

interview.question: When would you use re.fullmatch instead of re.search?
interview.answer: Use fullmatch when the entire string must match the pattern, such as validating a whole date or identifier. search returns a match if the pattern is found anywhere, so it can accept strings with extra text before or after.
interview.explanation: Anchoring with ^ and $ is the alternative, but fullmatch states the intent more clearly.

interview.question: What is the difference between greedy and lazy quantifiers?
interview.answer: A greedy quantifier such as + consumes as many characters as possible while still allowing the rest of the pattern to match. Adding ? makes it lazy, so it consumes as few as possible. The match is the same only when the surrounding pattern forces it.
interview.explanation: A classic example is matching tags or quoted text, where <.*> grabs too much and <.*?> stops at the first closing angle bracket.

interview.question: Why should regular expression patterns be raw strings?
interview.answer: In a normal string Python processes backslash escapes before the regex engine sees the pattern, so \d might become an unexpected character. A raw string r'\d' passes the backslash and letter through unchanged, making the pattern exactly what you typed.
interview.explanation: This is a frequent source of subtle bugs; raw strings exist precisely for patterns and filesystem paths.

interview.question: How can a regular expression cause a performance problem?
interview.answer: Nested quantifiers such as (a+)+ can make the engine try exponentially many ways to match a failing input, called catastrophic backtracking. Keep patterns specific, avoid nesting ambiguous quantifiers, and use simple string operations when they are enough.
interview.explanation: Mention that some engines use different algorithms, but Python's re can be vulnerable, so testing with worst-case inputs matters.

import re

n = int(input())
for _ in range(n):
    line = input()
    numbers = re.findall(r'-?\d+', line)
    print(' '.join(numbers) if numbers else 'none')

questions.topic: Built-in Data Structures: Lists, Tuples, Sets and Dictionaries
questions.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple?
questions.answer: A list is mutable and typically holds homogeneous items you will change; a tuple is immutable, often holds a fixed record, and being hashable it can be a dictionary key or set member if its elements are hashable.
questions.explanation: Mention that immutability makes tuples safe to share and slightly cheaper to create, though speed is rarely the deciding factor.

questions.topic: Built-in Data Structures: Lists, Tuples, Sets and Dictionaries
questions.question: Why is checking membership in a set faster than in a list?
questions.answer: A set is built on a hash table, so membership computes the hash of the value and checks a bucket, which is O(1) on average. A list must compare against items one by one and is O(n).
questions.explanation: The same hashing explains fast dictionary key lookups; note that worst-case behaviour can degrade if hashes collide.

questions.topic: Built-in Data Structures: Lists, Tuples, Sets and Dictionaries
questions.question: Why can't a list be used as a dictionary key?
questions.answer: Dictionary keys must be hashable, and hashability requires an object whose hash never changes. A list can be mutated, so its hash could change and break the mapping. Use a tuple instead.
questions.explanation: This links to __hash__ and __eq__ being defined together; mutable containers deliberately set __hash__ to None.

questions.topic: Built-in Data Structures: Lists, Tuples, Sets and Dictionaries
questions.question: How do you remove duplicates from a list while keeping order?
questions.answer: Build a set for fast membership and collect items in a new list only the first time they appear, for example dict.fromkeys(items) in Python 3.7+, or a loop with a seen set. A plain set(items) removes duplicates but loses the original order.
questions.explanation: dict.fromkeys is a neat one-liner because dictionaries preserve insertion order and the keys are unique.

questions.topic: Built-in Data Structures: Lists, Tuples, Sets and Dictionaries
questions.question: What is the average time complexity of common operations on these structures?
questions.answer: List indexing is O(1), list search is O(n), and appending is amortised O(1). Set and dict membership, insertion and deletion are O(1) on average. Sorting any of them is O(n log n).
questions.explanation: Interviewers like candidates who can map a data structure choice to the expected complexity rather than guessing.
